summary: B is preferable because it provides substantially better contract-focused verification, especially an end-to-end 429 retry that confirms the multipart payload survives replay. Both implementations share the same important design defect: Upload bypasses FilesService.Add despite the explicit requirement to route through it.
reasons: B verifies the multipart media type, field name, uploaded filename, and exact content; A never checks the uploaded content.

B exercises Upload through an actual 429 retry and verifies the content on both attempts. A only adds a generic retry-transport test using a bytes.Reader, which does not prove Upload produces a replayable request.
B tests empty-filename and nil-content validation and confirms no request is made; A adds no validation coverage.
Both correctly reuse multipartbody.NewFile and preserve the existing Add signature and behavior.
risks_a: Upload duplicates Add's option handling, request construction, decoding, and missing-data error instead of calling Add, violating the frozen contract.
No Upload-specific retry test, validation test, or source-reader error test.
The multipart test does not verify file content.
risks_b: Upload also duplicates Add rather than routing the encoded body through Add, violating the frozen contract and creating two implementations to maintain.
It lacks the required source-reader failure test.

The retry test supplies a bytes.Reader rather than an explicitly non-replayable/streaming source reader, so it does not fully demonstrate that buffering fixes the reported os.File-style case independently of source replayability.
